title: The monster hunted
text: In 1866 sailors all over the world report an enormous thing at sea: long, spindle-shaped, sometimes glowing, and far bigger and faster than any whale. At first it is a craze for cafés and newspapers. Then it turns dangerous. In 1867 it strikes the Cunard steamer Scotia below the waterline and leaves a clean triangular hole in her iron hull. Every unexplained wreck is now blamed on the "monster", and the public wants it destroyed.

The narrator, Professor Pierre Aronnax of the Paris Museum, is in New York when the story breaks. He publishes his theory that the culprit is a giant narwhal with a tusk like a ram. When the United States fits out the frigate Abraham Lincoln under Commander Farragut to hunt it, Aronnax accepts a place aboard at once, along with his calm, devoted servant Conseil. Also aboard is Ned Land, a Canadian known as the King of Harpooners, the one man on the ship who does not believe in the monster.

For months the frigate searches the Pacific in vain, until the crew is close to mutiny. On the last night of a final three-day reprieve, Ned sights the thing. It glows, circles the ship and outruns it through a full day's chase, and a cannon shell bounces off its hide. That night Ned harpoons it as it lies still. The harpoon rings as if it has hit something hard, a violent collision cripples the frigate, and Aronnax is thrown into the sea.

Conseil jumps in after his master, and the two swim for hours as the disabled frigate drifts away. Close to drowning, they are hauled onto the "monster" by Ned, who was thrown overboard too. Its back is made of riveted steel. The creature that puzzled the world is an underwater boat built by human hands. As chapter 7 ends, the boat starts to sink beneath them at dawn, and silent masked crewmen drag the three men down inside.

title: Aboard the Nautilus
text: A frigate sent to hunt a sea monster that was sinking ships found that the "monster" was a steel submarine. Its three survivors are Professor Aronnax, the narrator; Conseil, his unflappable servant; and Ned Land, a Canadian harpooner. They were dragged inside and locked in a dark iron cell. Two men came to look at them and seemed to understand none of the languages they tried. A silent steward brought a fine meal on dishes marked with an N and the motto "Mobilis in Mobili." After hours with no food, Ned lost his temper and throttled the steward, until a voice told him calmly, in French, to stop.

The voice belongs to the commander, the tall stranger from before, who speaks their languages perfectly and has simply been judging them. He calls himself Captain Nemo, Latin for "no one", and his ship is the Nautilus. He says he has broken with society and obeys none of its laws. The three may live aboard and move about freely, but they must accept being confined whenever he says, and since they now know his secret they can never go home. Ned refuses to promise not to escape. Nemo never asked him to.

Nemo shows Aronnax a floating palace: a library of 12,000 books, a lounge full of paintings, music and priceless shells and pearls, and an engine room. Everything runs on electricity he makes from seawater, and everything they eat and wear comes from the sea. He explains how the ship dives and steers, how its beacon made the famous glow, and how he built it in secret on a deserted island. He says ramming the Scotia was an accident and attacking the frigate was self-defense. He also claims to be almost endlessly rich.

Aronnax is torn between the loss of his freedom and the scientist's dream of seeing the ocean depths. As chapter 14 ends, the voyage officially begins off Japan on November 8, and the lounge panels slide open on the fish of the Black Current.

title: Across the Pacific
text: Professor Aronnax, his servant Conseil and the harpooner Ned Land went hunting a sea monster and found a submarine instead. Now they are passengers on the Nautilus, guests of the brilliant, secretive Captain Nemo, who has cut himself off from the world. They may go anywhere aboard, but they may never leave.

The voyage across the Pacific is full of wonders. In diving suits Aronnax and Conseil walk with Nemo across the seafloor to an underwater forest. They hide flat on the sand while sharks pass over them. They see the freshly sunk Florida with its dead still on deck. At Vanikoro, Nemo shows Aronnax the wreckage of the explorer La Pérouse's ships, and proof he found himself of how the last survivors died. Nemo's sympathies are hard to read. He loves the sea with passion, scorns the world above, and talks of the earth needing new men, not new continents.

In the reef-choked Torres Strait the Nautilus runs aground, and Nemo calmly waits for the full-moon tide. He lets the three go ashore, and they feast on fruit and game until islanders drive them back with stones and arrows. Hundreds of Papuans then surround the stranded ship. Nemo will not have any of them killed. He electrifies the railing to throw back the boarders, and the Nautilus floats free at exactly the hour he predicted.

In the Indian Ocean something on the horizon throws Nemo into a rage. He has the three locked in their old cell, and they fall into a drugged sleep. When Aronnax wakes, a haggard Nemo asks him, as a doctor, to see a crewman with a smashed skull, hurt in what Nemo calls a collision. The man dies in the night. As the First Part closes at chapter 24, the three have watched Nemo and his crew bury him in a hidden coral cemetery on the seafloor, where, Nemo says, their dead are safe "of sharks and men!"

title: Treasure in Vigo Bay
text: Professor Aronnax, Conseil and Ned Land are captives in all but name aboard the Nautilus, the submarine of the mysterious Captain Nemo. In the Indian Ocean Nemo locked them up and drugged them during an unexplained encounter, and a crewman died of his wounds and was buried on the seafloor. Aronnax now wonders whether the ship serves some scheme of revenge. Still, he wants to finish this tour of the world's seas, and he puts off Ned whenever the harpooner talks of escape.

Off Ceylon, Nemo takes them to walk the pearl beds. There he saves a poor Indian diver from a shark, is saved in turn by Ned's harpoon, and gives the stunned fisherman a bag of pearls. In the Red Sea, which seems a dead end, Nemo steers the ship through a secret underground passage, the Arabian Tunnel, into the Mediterranean.

With Europe so close, Ned forces Aronnax to agree that they will escape at the first sure chance. But Nemo keeps away from land. Near Crete Aronnax watches him signal to a diver and send off a chest of gold worth millions. Then Nemo takes the ship into a boiling undersea eruption off Santorini, and races across the Mediterranean in two days, deep and out of sight, before slipping out past Gibraltar.

Off Spain, Ned fixes the escape for nine o'clock one cloudy night. Waiting for the signal, Aronnax sees portraits of fighters for freedom and for oppressed peoples in Nemo's room. Just before the hour, the ship stops in the Bay of Vigo. Nemo shows him crewmen in diving suits gathering gold from Spanish galleons sunk there in 1702: this is where his wealth comes from. When Aronnax says such riches help no one, Nemo flares up about "victims to avenge" and breaks off. As chapter 32 ends, the escape has been ruined, and Aronnax guesses that the gold sent off near Crete went to the island's rebels.

title: Trapped under the ice
text: Professor Aronnax, Conseil and Ned Land have now spent months as Captain Nemo's captives aboard the Nautilus. They have seen wonders and glimpsed Nemo's private side: his hidden wealth from sunken treasure, his gifts to the oppressed, and flashes of anger at the world above. Ned's escape off Spain was spoiled when the ship stopped in Vigo Bay and then headed away from Europe.

Nemo takes Aronnax alone on a night walk across the Atlantic floor, lit by an underwater volcano, to the ruins of Atlantis. In a hidden harbor inside an extinct volcano his men mine coal to power the ship. The Nautilus crosses the weed-choked Sargasso Sea and dives to a record depth. Then it heads south, and hope of escape fades. Ned grows sullen. Nemo forbids him to hunt harmless whales, then uses the ship's steel spur to slaughter a pack of sperm whales, and Ned's dislike of the captain hardens.

Nemo forces the ship through the Antarctic ice and then beneath the great Ice Bank into open water beyond. On the equinox he fixes the sun at noon, declares that they stand at the South Pole, and claims it in his own name under a black flag marked with a gold N.

Heading back north under the ice, the Nautilus is knocked over by a capsizing iceberg and sealed in a tunnel of ice, with air for only two days. Crew and captives dig in shifts while the water around them starts to freeze. Aronnax nearly dies before Ned and Conseil give him the last of their air. As chapter 40 ends, the ship has crushed its way down through the ice floor and then rammed up through the surface into fresh air.

title: The black flag
text: Professor Aronnax, Conseil and Ned Land are captives aboard the Nautilus, the submarine of Captain Nemo, who has turned his back on the world. They have crossed the Pacific, the Indian Ocean, the Mediterranean and the Atlantic with him, reached the South Pole, and barely escaped suffocation when the ship was trapped under the Antarctic ice.

The ship races north up the Atlantic past South America. In the Caribbean, giant squid jam its propeller. In the fight on the platform one crewman is carried off crying "Help!" in French, and Nemo saves Ned's life, then weeps for his lost man. When Aronnax asks him to free them, Nemo refuses outright: whoever boards the Nautilus must never leave it. He rides out a hurricane on the surface as if courting death, and the storm ends Ned's hopes of escaping near New York.

Off the coasts of Ireland and England, Nemo searches for one exact spot. There he shows Aronnax the wreck of the French warship Avenger, sunk there on that same date in 1794 rather than surrender. Then an unflagged warship opens fire on the Nautilus. Nemo hoists his black flag and calls it the ship of an accursed nation, though he will not say which. He cries that he is the oppressed, and that his oppressors have destroyed everything he loved: country, wife, children, father and mother.

All night he draws the warship on. At dawn, with the hatch slammed shut on the three friends' hopes of escape, he rams it below its armor and watches it sink with all hands. As chapter 45 ends, Aronnax sees him kneel and sob before a portrait of a young woman and two small children.
